items.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy compounds a patient-specific NONPRESERVED aqueous oral suspension. The formula meets the USP <795> default requirements for this dosage form, which would ordinarily allow up to a 14-day refrigerated BUD in the absence of better data. However, specific trustworthy stability data for THIS formulation establish that potency falls below specification after FIVE refrigerated days. What BUD should the pharmacist consider?

choices.text: Fourteen days because the chapter's default BUD is a guaranteed minimum regardless of demonstrated instability.
choices.why: Incorrect. A default table maximum never overrides an earlier demonstrated stability failure for that actual formulation.

choices.text: No more than five refrigerated days, subject to all other applicable limits, rather than the longer default period.
choices.why: Correct. USP <795> Table 4 says a shorter BUD is required where the actual formulation's chemical or physical stability is shorter.

choices.text: Thirty-five days because this preparation is aqueous and all aqueous liquids have the preserved-formulation category BUD.
choices.why: Incorrect. The 35-day default applies to properly preserved aqueous dosage forms, not this nonpreserved suspension.

choices.text: Use the supplier's longest unexpired ingredient date, even if the finished mixture fails stability earlier.
choices.why: Incorrect. Ingredient shelf life is not proof of final compounded-formulation stability.

items.citation: USP <795> §10/Table 4 (official Nov. 2023, shorter stability governs); 247 CMR 9.01(3)
items.novelty_note: Adds a product-specific stability limit to the prior default-table question; current full USP normative text must be checked before approval.

items.stem: A Massachusetts sterile-compounding pharmacy plans to make a Category 2 injectable preparation. The active ingredient is a NONSTERILE bulk powder, but the diluent and receiving IV bag are sterile. The technician proposes mixing in an ISO Class 5 hood and then treating the preparation as though it was compounded only from sterile ingredients, without any sterilization step. What is the best response?

choices.text: Accept the plan because mixing a nonsterile powder inside ISO Class 5 air instantly converts it to a sterile starting ingredient.
choices.why: Incorrect. Cleanroom air is not a sterilization method, and the starting powder remains a nonsterile component.

choices.text: Use an appropriate validated sterilization approach (such as a suitable sterilizing filtration process or terminal sterilization) and apply the related release/BUD conditions before considering dispensing.
choices.why: Correct. USP <797> recognizes nonsterile starting components but requires an appropriate sterilization process and assessment of endotoxin and other risks.

choices.text: Select the longest Category 2 BUD because one sterile ingredient and one sterile bag outweigh the nonsterile powder.
choices.why: Incorrect. The presence of any nonsterile starting component affects controls, sterilization requirements and BUD eligibility.

choices.text: Label the final bag sterile solely because the pharmacist signs the compounding record, even without validating processing.
choices.why: Incorrect. A sign-off does not replace the sterile process and required release checks.

items.citation: USP <797> §§10.2, 11, 14 (official Nov. 1, 2023) and USP official FAQ on sterilization; 247 CMR 9.01(3)
items.novelty_note: Practical sterilization-vs-ISO5 misconception rather than ordinary sterile-component BUD recall.

items.stem: A Massachusetts sterile-compounding facility receives a FINAL above-action-level VIABLE environmental monitoring result for its ISO Class 7 BUFFER ROOM. A separate nonviable particle counter has not detected any excursion in the nearby ISO Class 8 room. The facility considers compounding during corrective action; no Board-specific instruction allowing longer BUDs has been issued. Which responses align with Board Policy 2026-03? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: Assess the viable excursion, implement remediation/CAPA, and arrange the required repeat environmental monitoring even if the separate nonviable count is normal.
choices.why: Correct. A normal nonviable result does not nullify the independent viable action level; policy §§III–IV require assessment, remediation and resampling.

choices.text: Continue ordinary long Category 2 BUDs because only the nonviable particles were within limits.
choices.why: Incorrect. The viable excursion triggers specific remedial limits, regardless of separate particle results.

choices.text: If the pharmacy resumes compounding during ISO 7 buffer-room remediation under policy conditions, limit applicable CSP BUDs to 24 hours room temperature or four days refrigerated.
choices.why: Correct. Board Policy 2026-03 §V expressly caps buffer-room BUDs during remediation, absent contrary Board direction.

choices.text: Declare the affected room fully cleared immediately because the ISO 8 area tested normally; resampling of the ISO 7 area is unnecessary.
choices.why: Incorrect. Affected-area repeat environmental monitoring and CAPA cannot be waived by an unrelated room's result.

items.citation: MA Board Policy 2026-03 §§III–VI (action-level environmental monitoring, adopted Sept. 3, 2026)
items.novelty_note: Distinguish viable action level from unrelated nonviable clearance evidence, with exact ISO7 buffer BUD cap.

items.stem: A Massachusetts retail pharmacy is registered as a DEA AUTHORIZED COLLECTOR with an approved collection receptacle. Three materials are presented on the same day: (X) a patient's lawfully held unused Schedule II tablets, (Y) expired Schedule II bottles that have never left the pharmacy's OWN inventory, and (Z) a partially used Schedule II dose generated by a hospital nursing unit. Which actions are appropriate as described? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: The patient may deposit the ultimate-user medication into the pharmacy's authorized collection receptacle using the collection procedures.
choices.why: Correct. 21 CFR 1317.75 permits qualifying ultimate users to deposit their own lawfully possessed controlled substances.

choices.text: The pharmacy may pour its expired Schedule II stock into the ultimate-user take-back receptacle to avoid reverse-distributor documentation.
choices.why: Incorrect. The authorized collection receptacle is not the lawful disposal route for the collector's own registrant inventory.

choices.text: The pharmacy must account for or transfer its own expired controlled stock through an appropriate registrant-disposal/reverse-distributor process instead of treating it as patient take-back.
choices.why: Correct. 21 CFR 1317.05(a), 1317.10 and applicable 1305 ordering/transfer rules govern registrant inventory disposal.

choices.text: The nursing unit may drop partially administered hospital controlled-substance remnants into the pharmacy's public ultimate-user receptacle as though they belonged to a patient.
choices.why: Incorrect. Institutional drug waste generated by a registrant is not simply an ultimate user's deposited medication; hospital controlled accountability/waste procedures apply.

items.citation: 21 CFR 1317.05(a), 1317.10, 1317.75(b)–(c); 21 CFR 1304.22 and applicable institutional accountability
items.novelty_note: Source ownership and location split: true ultimate-user deposit vs registrant inventory vs nursing unit waste.

items.stem: Two Massachusetts-licensed retail pharmacies participate in two distinct SHARED PHARMACY SERVICE workflows. In Workflow A, Pharmacy 2 remotely checks a prescription and performs claims adjudication but never physically fills or labels it; Pharmacy 1 fills and dispenses it. In Workflow B, Pharmacy 2 also physically fills and sends the labeled medication back to Pharmacy 1 for patient handoff. Under Board Policy 2021-02 revised February 2025, which statements are accurate? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: Workflow A is shared remote processing; Workflow B includes a central-fill activity because a second pharmacy physically prepares the patient's order.
choices.why: Correct. The policy defines central fill by physical preparation at the second pharmacy and delivery to the original pharmacy.

choices.text: Both arrangements automatically remove Pharmacy 1's liability for the prescription because Pharmacy 2 performed a portion of the work.
choices.why: Incorrect. The policy makes participants jointly responsible for properly processed or filled prescriptions.

choices.text: Both workflows need the required secure common record, audit trail, patient notice/opt-out when retail, training and joint procedures.
choices.why: Correct. Policy §III applies shared-service safeguards to all models; §IV has additional central-fill terms.

choices.text: A remote-only processing arrangement can skip consent and audit trails because no physical medication is transferred to the second site.
choices.why: Incorrect. The shared-service policy expressly covers remote processing and retains common safety and audit requirements.

items.novelty_note: Physical central fill vs cognitive remote processing; same retail notice/audit and joint accountability.

items.stem: A Massachusetts retail pharmacy stops dispensing for several days after flooding and uses its required COMPUTER-DOWNTIME plan while assessing damage. It then decides on November 1 to close PERMANENTLY on December 1. It has patient records and remaining controlled inventory, and served patients within the preceding 90 days. The manager proposes only to post a sign reading 'computer systems unavailable' and leave the records in the locked building after December 1. What is the best legal plan?

choices.text: Continue using the downtime plan without Board or patient closure notice, because the original cause was a flood.
choices.why: Incorrect. Once permanent closure is planned, 247 CMR 6.13 closure procedures supersede reliance solely on a temporary outage process.

choices.text: Follow the permanent-closure notice, patient-record transfer and controlled-inventory procedures, including applicable advance Board/patient notices, rather than only a downtime sign.
choices.why: Correct. The 30-day planning interval permits the statutory 14-day advance closure duties, patient access and controlled-substance handling, plus postclosure filings.

choices.text: Simply email previous patients on the closing date and destroy their medication profiles to protect privacy.
choices.why: Incorrect. Closure rules require advance patient notice and timely file transfers, not elimination of required records.

choices.text: Leave untransferred controlled stock locked indefinitely; the pharmacist's active personal registration authorizes holding it after pharmacy closure.
choices.why: Incorrect. Pharmacy closure entails compliant controlled stock transfer/disposal and return of licenses/registrations as required.

items.novelty_note: Transitions from true downtime into a planned permanent closure with 30 days' lead time.
